items.headline: Asia trades the morning-after of the Fed's first hike since 2023, with the dollar and Treasury yields firmer and BOJ next up Friday
items.detail: The Fed's unanimous 25bp move to 3.75%-4.00% landed after Asia's close on Wednesday, so Thursday's session was the region's first chance to reprice against it, and it did so through the dollar and rates channel rather than a straight equity selloff. The dollar index pushed to a roughly two-week high and US 10-year yields pushed toward 5%, dragging USD/JPY toward 156, USD/KRW toward 1,386 and keeping gold pinned near six-week lows around $4,300. Asian equities were mixed rather than uniformly weak -- Tokyo and Sydney rose on the weaker-currency, exporter-friendly read-through, while Hong Kong and Seoul fell as rate-sensitive tech and property names absorbed the higher-for-longer message and foreign investors trimmed exposure. The bigger swing factor for the region is now Friday: the Bank of Japan is close to a lock for a 25bp hike of its own, which would be its most hawkish policy pairing with the Fed since the BOJ began normalizing in 2024. Cross-asset desks are treating today largely as a positioning session ahead of that decision rather than a resolution of the hiking cycle question.
items.source: CNBC, Bloomberg, Saxo Bank Market Quick Take

items.headline: BOJ widely expected to hike 25bp to 1.25% on Friday, the highest Japanese rate since 1993
items.detail: All 52 economists surveyed ahead of the two-day meeting concluding September 18 expect the Bank of Japan to raise its policy rate a quarter point to 1.25%, which would be the BOJ's sixth hike since exiting ultra-loose policy in 2024 and its second this year. Roughly 93% of surveyed watchers expect a further move by January, with about a third pencilling in December, meaning tomorrow's decision is as much about the accompanying guidance and yen-support signalling as the move itself. The setup is unusual: a hawkish BOJ landing one day after a hawkish Fed compounds financial-conditions tightening for a region that is simultaneously nursing a weak yen, elevated oil-driven import costs and JGB 10-year yields near three-decade highs around 2.95%. Options and futures positioning in Nikkei and JGB markets has been building into the decision, and a explicit hike with dovish-leaning forward guidance would likely extend yen weakness and support exporters, while a hawkish surprise on the dot-plot-equivalent guidance would hit both JGBs and rate-sensitive Nikkei names hardest at Friday's open. The pairing of BOJ-Fed hikes this week is the first time both banks have tightened in the same calendar week since the BOJ's policy shift began.
items.time: Ahead of Friday Sept 18 decision (~03:00-06:00 UTC), preview circulated through Thursday's Asia session

items.headline: Hong Kong stocks fall roughly 1.1-1.2% as HKMA matches the Fed hike via the currency peg, Tencent and Alibaba both down
items.detail: The Hang Seng slid toward the 24,400-24,470 area, its worst level since around July, as the mechanical transmission of the Fed decision hit Hong Kong hardest of the major Asia markets. Because the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the US dollar, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority automatically matched the Fed's move, lifting its base rate 25bp to 4.25% overnight, which tightens local financial conditions in lockstep with the US regardless of Hong Kong's own domestic growth backdrop. Tencent fell about 1.6% and Alibaba about 1.5%, with the mega-cap tech complex leading losses as investors reassessed valuations against a higher discount rate and rising US-China trade risk. The move extends a rougher stretch for Hong Kong equities that has seen the index give back over 10% from this year's high, with desks flagging sticky oil-driven inflation and higher-for-longer messaging as the read-through into Chinese corporate earnings and property-sector refinancing costs. Mainland shares were comparatively more resilient than Hong Kong, underlining that the peg mechanism is doing much of the work in HK's underperformance today.

items.headline: Nikkei and Topix push through 64,200 as a weaker yen lifts exporters, even as Fed hike headlines dominate
items.detail: The Nikkei 225 added roughly 0.5-0.9% to trade above 64,200 (previous close 63,923), with the Topix up around 0.7-1% to near 4,100, as futures-led buying carried through from Wednesday's pre-Fed session. USD/JPY firming toward 156 -- its weakest yen level in about three sessions -- did the heavy lifting for exporter earnings translation, with SoftBank Group up roughly 1.2% and Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group up about 0.6%. The move is notable because it runs counter to the dollar-strength-equals-risk-off pattern seen in Hong Kong and Seoul today: Japan's exporter-heavy index structure means yen weakness is a net equity tailwind even as it signals tighter global financial conditions elsewhere. That dynamic is set to be tested directly at Friday's BOJ decision, where a hike (near-universally expected) paired with hawkish guidance could reverse the yen weakness that is currently propping up the Nikkei's gains. Desks are broadly treating today's strength as a 'buy the exporter trade before BOJ' positioning move rather than a durable repricing.
items.source: News On Japan, Sunday Guardian Live

items.headline: Kospi ends flat as foreigners dump a seventh straight session of large-cap chip stocks
items.detail: The Kospi closed essentially unchanged at 6,715.41 (-0.04%), giving back an intraday gain of more than 1% after foreign investors sold a net 2.28 trillion won (~$1.6bn), extending a seventh consecutive session of foreign outflows. The index opened firmly higher on the view that Fed-hike risk was already priced in, but turned negative in the afternoon as foreign funds rotated out of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix specifically, the two stocks with the heaviest index weight and the most direct exposure to global rate and AI-capex sentiment. The pattern is notable given both names sit at the centre of the memory supercycle story -- Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron are reportedly sold out of production capacity through 2027 -- suggesting today's selling is a rates/positioning story rather than a fundamental one. Local flow desks noted the won also stayed soft (USD/KRW near 1,386) despite the equity resilience, an unusual divergence that points to broad de-risking by offshore accounts around the Fed rather than Korea-specific news.

items.headline: SK Hynix rallies on Intel Ohio JV talks while top traders rotate out of Samsung after its HBM4 unveil
items.detail: SK Hynix was the most-bought name among Mirae Asset Securities' top-performing traders after reports it is in talks to lease part of the semiconductor fab Intel is building in Ohio to produce memory chips, with a broader joint venture involving SK Hynix, Intel and major cloud providers also reportedly under review. The same top-trader cohort was a net seller of Samsung Electronics, even though Samsung unveiled its next-generation HBM4 memory earlier this week in a bid to tighten its grip on AI-accelerator supply -- the market read is that the Intel tie-up gives SK Hynix a second high-margin growth vector (leading-edge foundry-adjacent capacity) that Samsung's product announcement alone doesn't offset. The story matters beyond single-name positioning: it signals capacity-constrained memory makers are now actively seeking JV and leasing structures with US foundries to meet AI-driven demand rather than relying purely on organic capex, a structural shift in how the memory supply chain is being built out. Both stocks remain central to Kospi's chip-heavy index composition and to the broader AI-capex trade that has driven much of this year's Asia tech outperformance.

items.headline: Shanghai Composite slips 0.4% to 3,877.46, mainland China lagging Japan's exporter-led bounce
items.detail: The Shanghai Composite fell about 0.4% to 3,877.46 on Thursday in direct reaction to the Fed's rate decision, a relatively contained move analysts described as largely priced in given the hike itself matched consensus. The pullback follows a stronger Wednesday session (Shanghai and CSI 300 both +0.7%, ChiNext +2%, STAR50 +4.1%) that had been driven by a tech-sector rally ahead of the Fed, so today's move is better read as a partial give-back than a fresh risk-off leg. The PBOC continued its steady-hand approach, fixing the USD/CNY reference rate stronger at 6.7580 (from 6.7628 previously) while keeping benchmark loan prime rates unchanged for a 15th straight month, reinforcing the central bank's 'supportive but stable' framing rather than reaching for stimulus. China's underperformance relative to Japan and Australia today underscores that mainland equities remain more sensitive to domestic property-sector and growth concerns than to the Fed's rate path directly, even as the broader dollar-strength backdrop still weighs on sentiment at the margin.

items.headline: ASX 200 rises 0.4% to 8,732 as RBA hike odds climb into the September 29 decision
items.detail: Australia's ASX 200 closed up around 0.4% at 8,732, extending its bounce off an 11-week low, even as the Fed's move added to pressure on the RBA to follow suit. NAB is now forecasting a 25bp RBA hike at the September 29 meeting to take the cash rate to 4.60%, while ANZ, CBA and Westpac all still expect the move in November, but all four major banks now agree a hike is coming before year-end. The RBA held at 4.35% in August while explicitly leaving the door open to further tightening, and July CPI at 3.5% y/y (trimmed mean 3.6%) remains well above the 2-3% target band, giving the hawks ammunition. AUD/USD was little moved on the day near 0.7221 (-0.01%), suggesting the RBA repricing is not yet a dominant driver of the currency relative to the broader dollar-strength theme from the Fed. The domestic policy debate is a genuine outlier in a region where most other central banks (BOJ, HKMA) are moving in lockstep with the Fed rather than debating their own independent cycle.

items.headline: Oil eases as Saudi Arabia routes crude around its damaged East-West pipeline, but the Hormuz/Red Sea chokepoint crisis stays unresolved
items.detail: WTI slipped about 0.2% to $102.14 and Brent eased to around $105.81, extending Wednesday's pullback as Saudi Arabia moves to cushion the impact of last weekend's drone-damaged East-West pipeline by making additional crude cargoes available to Asian refiners via ship-to-ship transfers near Oman's Sohar port. The pipeline, which has a 7mb/d design capacity and normally lets Saudi crude bypass the Strait of Hormuz entirely via the Red Sea port of Yanbu, remains a critical piece of regional supply infrastructure, and the workaround is a stopgap rather than a fix. The broader chokepoint crisis has not de-escalated: Houthi forces have reportedly taken the Red Sea port city of Mocha and the island of Perim near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, tightening their grip on a key backup shipping route just as the primary Hormuz corridor remains under threat from the wider Iran-linked conflict. For Asia specifically, oil is a genuine two-way risk this week -- a further escalation would hit import-heavy economies (Japan, India, Korea) hardest via both the trade balance and inflation channels, while today's partial reprieve is providing only temporary relief to refiners and current-account-sensitive currencies.

items.headline: Copper's Yangshan premium jumps to a near four-year high as Chinese buyers restock on the price dip
items.detail: The Yangshan copper premium, the standard gauge of Chinese physical demand for imported copper, rose 7% to $118 per tonne, its highest level in almost four years, even as LME three-month copper itself has pulled back about 4% from last week's record high near $14,875/t to trade around $14,231/t. The divergence is the story: Chinese buyers are using the pullback from record prices to rebuild inventory rather than stepping back, a signal of genuine underlying demand rather than speculative froth, and a read-through for industrial metals broadly as China's property-linked demand has otherwise been a persistent drag this year. The move comes against a backdrop of a structurally tight global copper market -- analysts have flagged a 17-year global supply shortage colliding with near-$110 oil and record smelter margins pressure -- meaning any sustained pickup in Chinese import demand has outsized price implications given how little spare mine and smelter capacity exists to absorb it. For multi-asset desks, the copper/Yangshan signal is one of the cleaner reads on Chinese real-economy demand available intraday, largely uncorrelated with today's equity-index-level Fed reaction.
items.time: LME/Yangshan pricing, most recent as of Sept 16-17 Asia trade

items.headline: Gold holds below $4,300, near six-week lows, as the post-Fed dollar and real yields weigh
items.detail: Spot gold traded in a roughly $4,294-$4,356 range and stayed below the psychologically important $4,300 handle for a second straight session, its lowest level in nearly six weeks, as the firmer dollar and rising Treasury yields following the Fed's hike removed some of the safe-haven bid that had been supporting the metal through the Middle East escalation. The pullback is notable given gold had been one of the primary beneficiaries of the chokepoint crisis narrative over the past two weeks; today's move suggests that, for now, the rates/dollar channel from the Fed decision is dominating over the geopolitical safe-haven channel. Asia dealers noted physical demand in India and China provided some support on dips given the softer local-currency gold price, but not enough to push spot back above $4,300 intraday. The metal remains up sharply on the year and well within its recent $4,270-$4,760 range, so today's move reads as consolidation into the BOJ decision rather than a trend reversal.

items.headline: PBOC fixes yuan stronger at 6.7580, holds LPR steady for a 15th straight month
items.detail: The People's Bank of China set its daily USD/CNY reference rate at 6.7580, firmer than the prior fix of 6.7628, a modest signal of currency stability management even as the dollar strengthened broadly post-Fed. USD/CNH in the offshore market traded around 6.7070, holding in a tight 6.7057-6.7141 range through the session. The central bank left both the one-year (3.0%) and five-year (3.5%) loan prime rates unchanged for a 15th consecutive month, in line with expectations and consistent with its stated 'supportive but moderately loose' stance. The steady fix and unchanged rates suggest the PBOC continues to prioritize currency and financial stability over an aggressive growth push, leaving fiscal policy and targeted property-sector measures as the primary growth levers for now.
items.time: PBOC fix ahead of Thursday's session, ~01:30 UTC

items.headline: India holds up best among Asia majors: Nifty +0.37%, rupee near flat despite the Fed hike
items.detail: The Nifty 50 rose about 0.37% to 23,303.55 and the Sensex added roughly 0.16% to 74,456.42 by midday, with Bharat Electronics, Bajaj Finance and Eternal leading gainers, while USD/INR held nearly flat around 95.95-95.99. India's relative resilience versus Hong Kong and Korea today fits a pattern this year of India being viewed as comparatively insulated from direct China/Hong Kong-style rate-peg mechanics and from the Korea/Taiwan chip-cycle volatility, leaving it more exposed to its own domestic earnings and RBI policy path than to today's Fed-driven cross-asset moves. FII flow data will be the key thing to watch over the next few sessions to see whether this resilience holds once the initial post-Fed dust settles.

items.headline: Asia credit spreads hold near multi-year tights; stress still concentrated in China property high yield
items.detail: The JACI (JP Morgan Asia Credit Index) spread tightened roughly 4bp to 82bp on a trailing weekly basis, near multi-year tight levels that reflect investors becoming more comfortable with regional credit risk broadly and accepting less compensation for it. The exception remains mainland China property and other idiosyncratic single-name credits, where the high-yield universe has structurally shrunk -- non-investment-grade active issuers have fallen from 136 in 2020 to just 22 in 2026 -- as defaulted or restructured names have been worked through and survivors skew toward stronger balance sheets. Desks are flagging a busy primary issuance calendar for the rest of September as the main near-term risk to spread stability, alongside the broader macro overhang from robust US data and hawkish Fed commentary that has raised the bar for continued spread compression. For fixed income allocators, the setup argues for staying selective in China property/HY exposure while broader Asia IG and quasi-sovereign credit continues to grind tighter.
items.source: Macrostream (Asia Credit Weekly), UBS Asset Management
items.time: Weekly context, as of Asia trade September 17

items.headline: JGB 10-year yield holds near three-decade highs around 2.95% into Friday's BOJ decision
items.detail: Japan's 10-year government bond yield has been oscillating in a roughly 2.93-2.98% band over the past week, close to its highest level in about three decades, as the market prices in Friday's near-consensus BOJ hike alongside a broader global steepening move tied to elevated US yields post-Fed. The level matters less as a single data point than as the backdrop against which the BOJ decision will land: a hike with hawkish forward guidance risks pushing yields decisively through the 3% threshold, a level that has previously triggered BOJ market-operation responses when crossed too quickly. Curve and duration desks are watching the JGB auction calendar and the BOJ's own bond-buying pace closely into the decision, given how sensitive both domestic bank balance sheets and the broader yen-funding trade are to a disorderly move in Japanese long rates.

items.headline: China's CXMT and SMIC keep gaining share in the memory and foundry supply chain
items.detail: Chinese memory maker CXMT has reportedly reached roughly 10% global DRAM market share with revenue up around 870% as it ramps mass production of LPDDR6 and HBM3E chips, while SMIC continues to post strong growth as China's domestic foundry alternative amid ongoing US export-control pressure on advanced chipmaking tools. The trend sits alongside -- and is partly a response to -- the capacity crunch at Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, all of which are reportedly sold out of memory production through 2027 as AI-driven demand outstrips supply; a faster-than-expected ramp from Chinese suppliers would be a genuine medium-term competitive threat to the Korean/US-aligned memory oligopoly, even if near-term technology gaps in HBM remain meaningful. For investors in the Korean and Taiwanese tech complex, this is a slower-moving but structurally important story to track alongside the day-to-day AI-capex headlines.
items.time: Ongoing story, context as of mid-September 2026

items.headline: New Zealand Q2 GDP beats forecasts at +0.2% q/q despite Middle East-linked drag
items.detail: New Zealand's economy grew a seasonally adjusted 0.2% in Q2, ahead of both the 0.1% consensus forecast and the RBNZ's own forecast of no growth, with annual growth of 2.6% also beating the 2.2% expected. Statisticians and RBNZ commentary flagged that the Middle East crisis's impact on trade and energy costs weighed on the quarter even as the headline print surprised to the upside, keeping the data more of a modest positive than a clear all-clear. The release was effectively the lone standalone data point of note on an otherwise quiet Asia economic calendar today, with FOMC digestion dominating cross-asset attention instead; NZD firmed modestly on the beat. RBNZ rate-path implications are limited near-term given the bank's own more cautious growth forecast was beaten only marginally, but the print reduces the probability of near-term RBNZ easing at the margin.

items.headline: BoE holds at 3.75% in a 6-3 split vote as gilts whipsaw from near-GFC-era highs to a sharp post-decision rally, sterling extends its slide
items.detail: The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to hold Bank Rate at 3.75%, with the three dissenters pushing for an immediate 25bp hike to 4.00% on the back of inflation running well above the 2% target. Going into the decision, gilts had already sold off hard on the combination of energy-driven inflation risk and fiscal anxiety ahead of Chancellor Healey's October 28 Budget: the 30-year yield touched 5.89% intraday, its highest since 1998, and the 10-year briefly traded near 5.25%, a level last seen around the global financial crisis. The decision itself triggered a sharp reversal -- the 10-year fell about 8bp to roughly 5.22% and the 30-year dropped nearly 12bp to about 5.74% -- as the BoE also announced it would pause gilt sales for six months and halt long-dated gilt sales entirely, laying out a multi-year plan to offload its remaining ~£488bn QE portfolio by 2034 rather than dumping duration into an already-stressed market. Sterling did not get the same relief: GBP/USD extended its post-Fed slide to around 1.3381 (-0.23%) as markets read the hold-with-hawkish-dissent outcome as delaying rather than removing tightening, with money markets now pricing an 80% probability of a November hike. For fixed income and rates desks this is the clearest cross-asset event of the European session -- a policy decision that moved gilts, sterling and the technical supply picture simultaneously, with direct read-through into the fiscal-headroom debate ahead of the Budget.
items.time: BoE decision ~11:00 UTC / noon London; gilt reaction through the London morning-afternoon

items.headline: European equities rally broadly as Fed-hike relief meets a genuine oil-driven inflation reprieve -- Stoxx 600 +0.4%, DAX and CAC both +0.6%, periphery outperforms
items.detail: The pan-European Stoxx 600 added about 0.4%, with the Euro Stoxx 50 up 0.57% to 6,272, Germany's DAX up roughly 0.6%, France's CAC 40 up 0.62% to 8,141, Spain's IBEX 35 up 0.44% to 19,721 and Italy's FTSE MIB up 0.32% to 52,080 -- a genuinely broad-based advance rather than a narrow single-sector pop. Two distinct forces are compounding: first, the Fed's Wednesday hike was largely priced in, so Thursday's session reads as relief that the decision is behind markets; second, and more important for Europe specifically, Brent crude fell to around $102-104 (down roughly 2.1%-2.7% over two sessions) after Saudi Arabia signalled it could restore part of the drone-damaged East-West pipeline's capacity within days and full operations within about six weeks, directly easing the energy-cost input that has been driving European inflation fears all month. The dollar hit a seven-week high on the belt of the Fed decision, which is providing an additional earnings-translation tailwind for European exporters. Desks are also citing unconfirmed Middle East de-escalation chatter as adding to the risk-on tone, though nothing concrete has been confirmed through official channels. The combination of falling energy costs, a resolved Fed decision and a firmer dollar is the dominant cross-asset narrative of the European session, touching equities, currencies, rates and commodities all at once.
items.source: Euronews, Investing.com, Estrategias de Inversión, Bolsamania

items.headline: Bilfinger craters 24% after slashing 2026 guidance and unveiling a 1,500-job restructuring, blaming Middle East-driven client caution
items.detail: German industrial services group Bilfinger fell more than 24% by mid-morning after cutting its 2026 revenue guidance to €5.3bn-€5.7bn from €5.4bn-€5.9bn and slashing its EBITA margin target to 3.2%-3.6% from 5.8%-6.2% (4.6%-5.0% adjusted for one-offs). Management pointed to a sudden, marked increase in customer caution during Q3 that hit both new contract awards and drawdowns under existing framework agreements, tying the pullback directly to the prolonged Middle East conflict weighing on client capex decisions across the industrial and energy-services complex the company serves. The board approved a restructuring programme dubbed 'Agile' that could affect up to 1,500 positions worldwide, requiring about €75m in one-off Q4 provisions against an expected €75m in annual savings once fully phased in from 2028. The move is a useful read-through for industrial-services and engineering names with Gulf-region exposure: it suggests the Middle East conflict is now showing up as a genuine demand-destruction story in European corporate earnings, not just a commodity-price and risk-sentiment overlay.

items.headline: Raiffeisen Bank International slides as much as 9% after Grizzly Research alleges $1.2bn in Russia sanctions-evasion trade
items.detail: Short-seller Grizzly Research published a report disclosing a short position in Raiffeisen Bank International and alleging the Vienna-based lender's Russian subsidiary was a central conduit for circumventing Western sanctions, citing customs records purportedly linking roughly $1.19bn in sanctioned goods trade to the bank. The report also flagged RBI's 2023 sale of Belarusian lender Priorbank to an Abu Dhabi shell company at around 60% below book value, characterising the deal as bearing hallmarks of sanctions circumvention. RBI shares fell as much as 9% on the day; the bank pushed back publicly, saying its compliance systems have been repeatedly reviewed since the start of the full-scale invasion and that the report contains factually wrong and misleading statements. This is a genuine single-name credibility event for one of the largest Austrian/CEE-exposed banks -- RBI has been the most closely watched Western lender still operating at scale in Russia -- and the allegations, if they gain regulatory traction, carry read-through risk for the broader CEE banking complex's Russia-exposure disclosures.
items.time: Vienna trade, through the London morning session

items.headline: Next raises profit guidance for a fourth time this year, shares jump over 3% on a strong UK consumer read
items.detail: UK retailer Next lifted its full-year 2026-27 pre-tax profit guidance by £12m to £1.255bn, the fourth upgrade this year, after first-half profit before tax rose 10.5% year-on-year to £569m on total full-price sales up 7.7%, aided by strong summer weather. Full-year EPS guidance was raised to 820.8p from 812.9p, implying roughly 10% annual EPS growth. Shares rose about 3.2% in early London trading. Management flagged a slowdown in expected second-half full-price sales growth to 5.8% from the first half's 7.7% pace, though that is still above the company's previous full-year forecast of 5.0%, so the guide is a genuine upgrade rather than merely a beat-and-hold. As one of the most closely watched UK consumer bellwethers, the repeated upgrade cadence is a useful counterpoint to the gilt-market fiscal-stress narrative dominating UK headlines today -- it suggests the domestic consumer has, so far, been resilient to the higher-for-longer rate backdrop and pre-Budget uncertainty.

items.headline: European bank stocks catch a post-Fed bid, reversing Tuesday's 1.3% Stoxx Banks slide, as JPMorgan's Q3 trading guidance sets a constructive read-through
items.detail: Bank shares outperformed across the region Thursday after JPMorgan forecast gains in third-quarter trading and investment-banking revenue, providing a constructive read-through for European lenders with sizeable capital-markets franchises. The move reverses part of Tuesday's roughly 1.3% decline in the Stoxx Europe Banks index, which had come as investors reassessed the balance between higher-for-longer rates (a net interest margin tailwind) against slowing loan growth, rising credit risk and a tougher macro backdrop. The sector remains a genuine swing factor for the broader European indices given its heavy index weighting, and today's bid sits alongside -- and is partly offset by -- the idiosyncratic Raiffeisen sell-off, underlining that bank-sector performance this week is being driven as much by single-name and US read-through dynamics as by a clean rates-repricing narrative.

items.headline: Brent falls toward $102-104 as Saudi Arabia moves to restore East-West pipeline capacity, easing Europe's energy-inflation channel
items.detail: Brent crude fell to around $102-103.6 a barrel, down roughly 2.1% on the day and extending a 2.7% drop in the prior session, after Saudi Arabia indicated it could restore about half of the drone-damaged East-West pipeline's capacity within days and reach full operations within roughly six weeks -- materially faster than the three-to-six-week (and in some analyst views, months-long) repair estimates that had circulated earlier in the week. The pipeline normally carries up to 5% of global oil supply from the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz entirely, so the restoration timeline is the single most important variable for the European energy-inflation outlook right now: a faster fix directly reduces the risk that oil-driven inflation forces the ECB, BoE or other European central banks into a more aggressive tightening path than currently priced. The flip side showed up in equities -- Stoxx Europe Energy dipped about 0.2% as the oil majors gave back some of their recent trading-windfall gains even as the broader market cheered lower input costs.

items.headline: USD/TRY grinds to a fresh record low near 48.67 as CBRT holds at 37% for a fifth straight meeting
items.detail: The Turkish lira weakened to a fresh record low near 48.67 per dollar, continuing the central bank's tolerated slow-devaluation path, as the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey held its policy rate at 37% for a fifth consecutive meeting, in line with expectations. The CBRT's statement said recent inflation data and leading indicators point to a decelerating underlying inflation trend and confirmed continued weakness in domestic demand, while explicitly flagging that surging energy prices tied to the escalation in the Iran-US/Middle East conflict are a heightened inflationary risk. The lira is now down roughly 18% over the past twelve months and 1.6% over the past month, a pace of depreciation the CBRT continues to manage rather than defend outright via FX intervention. For EM and periphery-Europe desks, Turkey remains the clearest example in the region of a central bank explicitly trading currency stability for a still-gradual disinflation path, with the Middle East energy-price channel now the dominant upside risk to that plan.
items.time: CBRT decision + FX trade through the session

items.headline: South African rand near a one-week low around 16.1-16.25/USD after Q2 GDP contraction ends a six-quarter expansion streak
items.detail: USD/ZAR held near a one-week low around 16.1-16.25, with the rand's recent softness tracing back to worse-than-expected domestic GDP data showing South Africa's economy contracted 0.2% in Q2, ending six consecutive quarters of growth, as the escalating Middle East conflict disrupted energy-intensive mining and manufacturing activity. SARB hiked its repo rate to 7% in May and held it there through July, with Governor Kganyago signalling the central bank can afford to respond cautiously to recent inflation shocks (inflation eased to 4.3% in July from 5% in June) even as August-September fuel price adjustments risk a temporary reversal. With municipal elections set for November 4, the rand's near-term path is as much a domestic political-risk story as a global dollar-strength one, and today's softness is best read as a continuation of that pre-existing trend rather than a fresh catalyst.

items.headline: Bund 10-year holds steady near 3.51% even as ECB signals more tightening ahead, a rare pocket of European rates calm
items.detail: Germany's 10-year Bund yield was little changed around 3.51%, up roughly 25bp over the past month but essentially flat on the day, a notable contrast to the volatility in UK gilts and US Treasuries this week. The steadiness comes despite the ECB having delivered its second hike of the year on September 10 (deposit rate to 2.50%, main refi to 2.65%), with officials citing renewed inflation risk from higher energy prices tied to the Middle East conflict; markets are now pricing the ECB deposit rate reaching roughly 2.9% by December, implying at least one more hike priced in before year-end. The relative Bund calm suggests the market views the ECB's tightening path as largely already communicated and priced, in contrast to the UK where today's BoE hold-with-hawkish-dissent outcome and the fiscal-headroom debate ahead of the October Budget are actively repricing the gilt curve.

items.headline: EUR/USD softer, dollar hits a seven-week high broadly as markets digest the Fed hike
items.detail: EUR/USD traded in a roughly 1.153-1.160 range through the session, with the euro on the back foot as the dollar index pushed to its highest level in about seven weeks following Wednesday's Fed hike and hawkish dot-plot guidance. EUR/GBP, by contrast, ticked up toward 0.8588 (GBP/EUR near 1.1655-1.1671), as sterling underperformed the euro on the day given the BoE's hold-with-dissent outcome versus an ECB that has already delivered its second hike of the year. The divergence -- euro weaker against the dollar but firmer against the pound -- is a clean illustration of today's core cross-asset theme: a broadly stronger dollar dominating G10 FX, with the BoE decision acting as the idiosyncratic swing factor for sterling specifically.

items.headline: Luxury sector stays under pressure: Hermès flat near €1,383, LVMH trading well off its 52-week high
items.detail: Hermès traded roughly flat around €1,383, within a €1,358.50-€1,389 day range and well below its 52-week high of €2,300, while LVMH (most recently quoted around €417, versus a 52-week high of €654.70) continues to trade near multi-month lows. The sector's underperformance this year reflects a structural rather than cyclical set of headwinds -- softer Chinese luxury demand, currency translation drag from a firmer dollar on European reporting, and general risk-off positioning in discretionary consumer names during a period of elevated rates. Analyst coverage remains broadly constructive on both names (heavy buy-rating skew with substantial theoretical upside on both stocks), suggesting the market is treating the pressure as a valuation reset rather than a fundamental deterioration, but neither stock has yet found a durable floor.

items.headline: European autos remain structurally under pressure from Chinese competition even as Volkswagen's restructuring plan draws support
items.detail: The broader European auto sector continues to wrestle with Chinese EV makers taking European market share, a theme flagged again in sell-side commentary this week describing valuations that assign little value to legacy automakers' core businesses despite improved cash flows and earnings. Volkswagen has been the relative outperformer after its supervisory board backed a turnaround plan including 50,000 additional job cuts, while Stellantis continues to lean on new-model launches (nine concept cars slated for the Paris Motor Show) and French-plant investment to defend share. No fresh today-specific single-name catalyst emerged in the sector during the European session, but the structural competitive story remains one of the more important slow-moving themes for European industrials allocators to track into year-end.
items.time: Ongoing story, context as of the European session

items.headline: Canada's Carney pitches EU 'associate membership' to European Parliament; Trump threatens to halt US-EU trade if it proceeds
items.detail: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, endorsing European Commission President von der Leyen's proposal to grant Canada 'associate member' status within the EU -- a novel institutional arrangement without recent precedent. President Trump responded by threatening to halt US trade with Europe entirely if Canada is admitted as an EU associate member, escalating an already tense transatlantic trade backdrop. The story has not yet shown up as a clean market-moving catalyst in European equities or FX today, but it adds another layer of trade-policy tail risk for EU-exposed exporters and is worth tracking closely given the administration's willingness to follow through on trade threats this year; multi-asset and macro desks should treat this as an emerging risk rather than a resolved one.
items.time: Strasbourg address, through the European afternoon

items.headline: Anglo American, Bollore and Dassault Systèmes post notable single-name moves without a clear broad-market driver
items.detail: Among the day's smaller single-name stories: Anglo American rose about 1.1%, tracking firmer industrial-metals sentiment consistent with the Chinese copper-restocking signal flagged in Asia trade; Bollore fell around 1.1%; and Dassault Systèmes dropped about 2.4%, with no single dominant catalyst identified across the newsflow scanned today. These moves sit below the bar for a standalone tradable theme but are worth noting for desks tracking index-constituent dispersion, particularly given how narrow the gap was between the day's broad indices (+0.2% to +0.9%) and the wider spread of single-name outcomes underneath them.

items.headline: USD/PLN and CEE FX stay choppy, zloty trading in a wide 3.72-3.81 weekly range
items.detail: The Polish zloty traded within a roughly 3.72-3.81 range against the dollar over the past week, with the largest single-day move (+0.73%) coming Wednesday around the Fed decision. There was no fresh Poland-specific catalyst identified in today's newsflow; the moves are consistent with the broader dollar-strength theme dominating G10 and EM FX post-Fed rather than any domestic National Bank of Poland policy shift. CEE currencies broadly remain a secondary read on the same US-dollar and European-rates cross-currents driving the rest of the session, without an independent local narrative today.
